To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
distributional measures of semantic distance have the ability to mimic both similarity and relatedness, but they perform poorly when compared to human judgment.

(i) distributional measures of similarity and relatedness are not as good as WordNet-based measures; (ii) distributional measures have a number of attractive features that WordNet-based measures lack; (iii) distributional measures can be brought more into line with human judgment by (a) incorporating a variety of measures and (b) using a variety of corpora; (iv) distributional measures are not necessarily more resource-poor than WordNet-based measures.

(1) distributional measures of semantic distance are more closely aligned to human judgment than previously reported; (2) distributional measures can be improved by taking the context into account, and (3) hybrid measures can improve the performance of distributional measures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How well do distributional measures of semantic distance mimic human judgment of semantic distance?
the following questions: (a) What are distributional measures of semantic distance?
the question: what are the best ways of estimating semantic distance from raw text?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
distributional measures of semantic distance are not as bad as they seem, and that they are not as good as WordNet-based measures.
the best measures of semantic distance are those that use a combination of knowledge sources, including distributional ones, and are tuned to specific tasks.
there is no single measure that outperforms others in every respect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of distributionally-based measures for semantic distance is not as hopeless as has been claimed.
distributional measures are not yet as effective as WordNet-based measures in estimating human notions of semantic similarity.
distributional measures of semantic distance have a lot of potential, but that they are not yet ready for prime time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
distributional measures of semantic distance can indeed be used as a proxy for human notions of semantic similarity.

distributional measures of semantic distance can be used as proxies for semantic distance when the resources required for WordNet-based measures are not available, but their use is limited to specific domains.
, although distributional measures are not as accurate as WordNet-based measures in estimating human judgments, they have a lot of potential and should not be dismissed as inferior measures.
